120	## Anti-patterns
121	
122	<!--skill-flavor:project-creation-antipatterns:start-->
123	- **Prefer running `uip maestro flow init` from inside the solution you named** — run outside one it auto-scaffolds `<Project>Solution/`, but the auto name won't match your chosen solution name. Never pass `--skip-solution-registration` for a project you intend to upload (it leaves a bare single-nested layout). See [SKILL.md rule #6](../../SKILL.md#critical-rules-universal) for the required double-nested `<Solution>/<Project>/<Project>.flow` layout and the self-check.
124	<!--skill-flavor:project-creation-antipatterns:end-->
125	- **Never guess node schemas** — use `registry get` for all node types. Guessed port names or input fields cause silent wiring failures.
126	- **Never guess the value or format of a business output** — when a request names an output (`caseKey`, `ticketId`, `severity`, …) without saying how to derive it, elicit the rule ([SKILL.md rule #5](../../SKILL.md#critical-rules-universal)) or confirm your assumption before building. Inventing a format — e.g. prefixing an id that should pass through unchanged — yields a flow that passes `flow validate` but returns the wrong business outcome at runtime. See rule #17 above.
127	- **Never skip capability discovery for connector nodes** — run `registry search` to confirm the connector exists and what operations it supports before building. See [connector/planning.md](references/plugins/connector/planning.md). Skipping this is the #1 cause of designing around a connector that doesn't exist or an operation it doesn't support.
128	- **Never replace a registered connector operation with `core.logic.mock` because configuration cannot run** — if `registry search` / `registry get` finds `uipath.connector.<connector-key>.<operation>`, add that real connector node via `uip maestro flow node add`. Missing live connections, missing tenant access, or prompts that ask you to only plan `--detail` mean: run `node add`, write the planned `--detail` payload to a sidecar file (e.g. `<nodeId>.detail.json`), and surface "configure pending" as an Open Question. **Do not leave a partial `inputs.detail` on the node** — the validator rejects hand-authored envelopes, and the node will not pass `flow validate` until `node configure` is run. Studio Web and reviewers need the real connector key in the `.flow`; the agent must report this explicitly rather than letting the user discover it via a later validation failure. See [§ Node ownership](#node-ownership--who-authors-the-node) and [connector/impl.md — No-Live-Tenant / Planned Configuration](references/plugins/connector/impl.md#no-live-tenant--planned-configuration).
129	- **Never set `inputs.errorHandlingEnabled: true` on a node with no outgoing `error` edge** — the flag is CLI-owned (`edge add --source-port error` and `flow format` derive it from the error edges actually present). A hand-set flag with no handler suppresses the node's fault, so the failure is swallowed and the run reports success. See rule #16 above.
130	- **Never route an `error` port back into the happy path** — an error edge into the next happy-path node, or into the same End node the success path reaches, makes every failed run report `Completed` with success-shaped outputs. Send it to a distinct End node with an error/status output, to `core.logic.terminate`, or to a branch that genuinely recovers.
131	- **Never edit `content/*.bpmn`** — it is auto-generated from the `.flow` file and will be overwritten.
132	- **Never use `core.logic.mock` when the resource is in the same solution** — use `--local` discovery instead. Mock placeholders are only for resources that are not in the current solution and not yet published.
133	- **Never hand-write `definitions` entries** — always copy from registry output. Hand-written definitions have wrong port schemas and cause validation failures.
134	- **Never put any `model` block on node instances** — BPMN type, serviceType, event definition, binding templates, and context templates all live in the node's **definition** (copied verbatim from `registry get` into `definitions[]`). Instances carry only per-instance data: `inputs`, `outputs`, `display`. Identity fields like `entryPointId` / `isDefaultEntryPoint` (triggers) and `color` / `content` (sticky notes) live under `inputs`. This applies to every inline-agent-related node too: `uipath.agent.autonomous` plus every attached `uipath.agent.resource.*` node (tool, escalation, context) carries source identity at `inputs.source = <UUID>`. Their definitions declare `model.source: true`; flow-core hoists onto the instance.
135	- **Never author `model.context[]` on resource-node instances** — resource-node instances have no `model` block. For `uipath.core.*` resource nodes (rpa, agent, flow, agentic-process, api-workflow, hitl), the definition (from `registry get`) already carries `model.context[]` with `<bindings.{name}>` placeholders. Your job is to add matching entries to the top-level `bindings[]` array — two entries per resource node (`name` + `folderPath`) with `resourceKey` matching the definition's `model.bindings.resourceKey`. At BPMN emit, the runtime rewrites `<bindings.{name}>` → `=bindings.{id}` via `(resourceKey, name)` matching. Without the top-level `bindings[]` entries, `uip maestro flow validate` passes but `uip maestro flow debug` fails with "Folder does not exist or the user does not have access to the folder." See the resource plugin's `impl.md`.
136	- **Never put a `ui` block on node instances** — position and size belong in the top-level `layout.nodes` object. Nodes with `"ui": { "position": ... }` use the wrong format and may not render correctly in Studio Web.
137	- **Never skip `flow format` before publish or debug** — without it, hand-written `layout` data renders as misshapen rectangles in Studio Web (the MST-9061 failure mode). See rule #12 above for the format step.
138	- **Never validate after every individual edit** — intermediate flow states (e.g., node added but not yet wired) are expected to be invalid. Run `uip maestro flow validate` once after the full build is complete.
139	- **Never use `console.log` in script nodes** — `console` is not available in the Jint runtime. Use `return { debug: value }` to inspect values.
140	- **Never forget output mapping on End nodes** — every `out` variable in `variables.globals` must have a `source` expression in every reachable End node's `outputs`. Missing mappings cause silent runtime failures.
141	- **Never update `in` variables** — only `inout` variables can be modified via `variableUpdates`. Input variables are read-only after flow start.
142	- **Never reference parent-scope `$vars` inside a subflow** — subflows have isolated scope. Pass values explicitly via subflow inputs.
143	- **Never use `core.action.http` (v1)** — the v1 node is deprecated for all HTTP requests (both connector-authenticated and manual). For connector-auth, v1's `authenticationType: "connection"` input does not pass IS credentials at runtime. Use `core.action.http.v2` (Managed HTTP Request) for every HTTP node. See [http/planning.md](references/plugins/http/planning.md).
144	- **Never hand-write `definitions[]` or `inputs.*` for managed HTTP nodes** — use `uip maestro flow node add` (with `--input` for `branches` / `timeout` / `retryCount`) and `uip maestro flow node configure` (for `inputs.detail`). These are the only supported authoring paths. Hand-written `definitions[]` strips required manifest fields; hand-written `inputs.detail` misses `essentialConfiguration` and fails at runtime. See [http/impl.md](references/plugins/http/impl.md).
145	- **Never write `$vars.X` (or `$metadata.X`, `$self.X`) without `=js:` in value fields** — `flow validate` flags this as MST-9107. See rule #11 above and [shared/node-output-wiring.md](../shared/node-output-wiring.md) for the per-node-type field reference.
146	- **Never reuse a reference ID (mailbox folder, Slack channel, Jira project, Google Sheet, etc.) from a prior flow or session** — reference IDs are scoped to the specific authenticated account behind the connection. A `parentFolderId` from one Outlook mailbox is invalid in another; a Slack channel ID from one workspace is invalid in another. A reused ID passes `flow validate` and `node configure` cleanly, then faults silently at runtime with no resolvable error. Always re-resolve via `uip is resources run list <connector-key> <objectName> --connection-id <CURRENT_CONNECTION_ID> --output json` against the connection bound to this flow — do not paste a value you saw in another flow. See [connector/impl.md — Step 4](references/plugins/connector/impl.md) and [connector-trigger/impl.md — Step 3](references/plugins/connector-trigger/impl.md).
147	- **Never include `[*]` literally in a connector `bodyParameters` / `queryParameters` / `pathParameters` key** — `[*]` in `requestFields[].name` is an array marker. Strip it and pass a `=js:` expression returning the array (e.g. `"fields.labels[*]"` → `"fields.labels": "=js:(['a', 'b'])"`). Never a literal JSON array — it validates but does not bind. Supported only when `[*]` is the name suffix; `[*]. See [connector/impl.md — Step 6b](references/plugins/connector/impl.md) for the full table including expression-value handling.

1	# Greenfield — Create a New Flow
2	
3	End-to-end journey for creating a Flow project from scratch. Author terminates at `validate` + `format`. To publish, run, or debug after this, see [operate/CAPABILITY.md](../../operate/CAPABILITY.md).
4	
5	> **Brownfield edits use a different journey.** If the `.flow` file already exists, see [brownfield.md](brownfield.md) instead.
6	
7	## Should you plan first?
8	
9	For complex flows, produce a plan before building. Reference [planning-arch.md](planning-arch.md) and [planning-impl.md](planning-impl.md) for the node type catalog, port reference, wiring rules, and topology patterns.
10	
11	**Plan when:**
12	- The flow has 5+ nodes with branching or parallel paths
13	- The flow uses connectors or resources that need discovery
14	- The user's requirements are ambiguous and you need to confirm the approach
15	
16	**Don't plan when:**
17	- Adding/editing a single node in an existing flow (use [brownfield.md](brownfield.md))
18	- The flow is a straightforward linear pipeline (trigger → action → action → end)
19	- The user has already described the exact topology they want
20	
21	### Examples
22	
23	**Plan:** "Build a flow that receives a Jira ticket, classifies it with an AI agent, routes urgent tickets to Slack and non-urgent to a queue, and logs everything to a Google Sheet."
24	→ Multiple services, branching logic, connector discovery needed. Plan first.
25	
26	**Don't plan:** "Create a flow that calls an API and sends the result to Slack."
27	→ Linear pipeline, user knows what they want. Build directly, ask questions inline if needed. **"Build directly" skips the plan doc, not the registry search** — you still `registry search` each named service and pick a node type via the Step 3 ladder.
28	
29	**Judgment call:** "Build me a flow that processes invoices."
30	→ Ambiguous requirements. Ask clarifying questions; plan if answers reveal complexity.
31	
32	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-execution-map-intro:start-->
33	## Three-turn execution map
34	
35	Steps 0–6 are **logical phases**, not separate turns. A typical greenfield build collapses to **three assistant turns** (universal SKILL.md rule #10). Each step heading below carries a `[T1]` / `[T2]` / `[T3]` tag — emit every tool call inside the same Turn as one assistant message.
36	
37	| Turn | Steps | What you emit in ONE assistant message |
38	|---|---|---|
39	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-execution-map-intro:end-->
40	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-t1-execution:start-->
41	| **T1 — Setup + discovery** | 0, 1, 2, 3 | One chained `Bash` (scaffold + register + pull + `node add` for each CLI-owned node) **+** parallel `Bash` (one `registry get` per OOTB type you'll inline) **+** parallel `Read` (plugin `impl.md`s). **If existing `.uipx` solutions are present, the Step 2 gate fires first in its own turn** — resolve it before this chain. |
42	| **T2 — Read + author** | 4 | One `Read` of the `.flow` **+** a batch of `Edit` calls (or one `Write` if ≥70% of nodes change). Claude Code serializes Edits on the same file, so they don't race |
43	| **T3 — Finalize** | 5, 6 | One chained `Bash` (`node configure && validate && format`). On validate failure: one Edit turn, then re-chain `validate && format` |
44	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-t1-execution:end-->
45	
46	### Batching anti-patterns
47	
48	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-init-batching:start-->
49	- **One CLI per turn.** Never issue `solution init`, then `cd`, then `flow init` as three separate Bash calls — chain with `&&`, the `cd` included as its own segment. Same for `node configure && validate && format`.
50	- **Sequential `registry get`s.** Emit every `registry get` as a parallel `Bash` in one message alongside the T1 scaffold chain.
51	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-init-batching:end-->
52	- **Validating after every Edit.** Validate once at the end of T3 (or after a recovery Edit). Intermediate states are expected to be invalid.
53	- **Re-reading the `.flow` every turn.** `Read` once at the start of T2; subsequent `Edit`s in the same conversation don't need re-reading unless an external command (e.g., `node configure`, `format`) rewrites the file between Edits.
54	- **`Edit` in the same turn as a `Bash` that mutates the same file.** Parallel tool calls race — separate them across turns.
55	- **Two parallel `Edit`s anchored to the same byte range.** Same-file Edits serialize in execution order; if Edit N's `old_string` overlaps text that Edit N-1's substitution removed or shifted, Edit N fails with "string not found." Use the [per-array anchor pattern](#anchoring-parallel-flow-edits--anchor-on-what-you-read-not-on-key-order) — anchor each Edit on its target array's own opening key, never on key order or a shared boundary.

85	## Step 2 — Create a solution, THEN a Flow project inside it **[T1]**

116	
117	### 2a. Create a new solution
118

121	```
122	
123	Creates `<cwd>/<SolutionName>/<SolutionName>.uipx`. **`cd` into the new solution directory before Step 2b.**

When solutions already exist and the user chooses "Create a new solution", **ask for the new solution's name** — do not reuse the project name (SKILL.md rule #6). The two names are independent.

127	### 2b. Create the Flow project inside the solution folder
128	
129	```bash
130	cd <directory>/<SolutionName> && uip maestro flow init <ProjectName> --output json
131	```
132

204	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-registry-transition:start-->
205	## Step 3 — Refresh the registry **[T1 — chained tail of Step 2]**
206	
207	This is already the last segment of the [canonical T1 chain](#canonical-t1-chain--issue-this-as-one-bash-call) above. Standalone:
208	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-registry-transition:end-->
209	
210	```bash
211	uip maestro flow registry pull                          # refresh local cache (expires after 30 min)
212	```
213	
214	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-end-node-discovery:start-->
215	**Parallel `registry get`** — in the same T1 assistant message, emit one separate `Bash` per OOTB node type whose definition you'll inline in T2. **Always fetch `core.control.end`** — `flow init` does not scaffold one (see Step 4):
216	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-end-node-discovery:end-->
217	
218	```bash
219	uip maestro flow registry get core.control.end --output json
220	```
221	
222	> **Auth note**: Without `uip login`, registry shows OOTB nodes only. After login, tenant-specific connector and resource nodes are also available. **In-solution sibling projects** are always available via `--local` without login — see below.
223	
224	### Select the node type for each external service (runs even when full planning is skipped)
225	
226	Calling a named external service (Slack, open-meteo, Stripe, any REST API)? **Search first — never guess the node type from the brand name:**
227	
228	```bash
229	uip maestro flow registry search "<service>" --output json --output-filter "[*].{NodeType:NodeType,DisplayName:DisplayName,Description:Description,AvailableOnTenant:AvailableOnTenant}"
230	```
231	
232	Then pick the first match down this ladder:
233	
234	1. **Curated connector activity** (`uipath.connector.<key>.<op>` in the results) → use it.
235	2. **Connector exists but no activity for what you need** → `core.action.http.v2` (connector mode).
236	3. **No connector at all** → `core.action.http.v2` (manual mode).
237	4. **No API** (desktop app) → [rpa](plugins/rpa/planning.md).
238	
239	Manual HTTP is the **bottom of the ladder** — only the search returning no connector authorizes it. Picking it without searching is the brand-name shortcut forbidden by [SKILL.md rule #3](../../../SKILL.md#critical-rules-universal).

241	### Document-extraction step — route it to IxP (runs even when full planning is skipped)
242	
243	Pulling **named fields out of documents** (PDFs, scans, receipts, invoices, contracts, forms) is a document-extraction step — its node is an **IxP node** (`uipath.ixp.*`). It's easy to miss because the fetch/post steps around it are ordinary nodes, but the extraction in between is its own node. **Always land a node for it — never leave it out:**
244	
245	- **Model published** → land the real `uipath.ixp.*` node (skeleton is fine; defer config to Open Questions).
246	- **No model published** (`registry search "uipath.ixp"` → `Data: []`) → land a `core.logic.mock`.
247	
248	See [plugins/ixp/impl.md — Landing the node when you cannot fully configure it](plugins/ixp/impl.md#landing-the-node-when-you-cannot-fully-configure-it).
249	
250	**In-solution discovery (no login required):**

253	uip maestro flow registry list --local --output json     # discover sibling projects in the same .uipx solution

255	uip maestro flow registry get "<node-type>" --local --output json  # get full manifest for a local node

258	Run from inside the flow project directory. Returns the same manifest format as the tenant registry. Use `--local` to wire in-solution resources (RPA, agents, flows, API workflows) without publishing them first. `search --local` omits `AvailableOnTenant` — drop it from `--output-filter` projections.

260	## Step 4 — Build the flow **[T2]**
261	
262	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-build-scaffold-assumptions:start-->
263	> **`flow init` scaffolds ONLY the manual trigger (`start` / `core.trigger.manual`) with zero edges.** Every other user-owned node — **including the End node** — is yours to add via `Edit` / `Write`. Any HTTP / connector / connector-trigger node you `node add`-ed in T1 is already in `nodes[]` and `definitions[]` but has empty `inputs.detail` (filled in T3) and is not wired yet.
264	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-build-scaffold-assumptions:end-->
265	
266	### T2 batch — issue these in ONE assistant message
267	
268	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-t2-read-source:start-->
269	1. **One `Read`** of `<ProjectName>.flow` — required before any Edit/Write; T1's chained Bash mutated the file and Claude Code's file-state tracker does not auto-refresh on external mutations.
270	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-t2-read-source:end-->
271	2. **A batch of parallel `Edit` calls** — one per top-level array you're modifying. Same-file Edits serialize in execution order, so each `old_string` must anchor to text NO OTHER parallel Edit modifies. Use the **per-array anchor pattern** below.
272	   - Edit `nodes[]` — add the End node (and any other user-owned nodes).
273	   - Edit `definitions[]` — paste the End definition verbatim from T1's `registry get core.control.end` output.
274	   - Edit `edges[]` — wire `trigger → <httpNode> → end`. End-node `outputs` mapping goes here too if you declared an `out` variable in `variables.globals`.
275	   - Edit `layout.nodes` — placeholder `{ position: { x: 0, y: 0 }, size: { width: 96, height: 96 }, collapsed: false }` per new node; `format` rewrites both position and size (by node shape) in T3.
276	
277	   `Write` of the whole file is allowed but token-costly on flows >~10 nodes — only fall back to `Write` when ≥70% of nodes change AND the file is small (see [editing-operations.md — Tool Selection Ladder](editing-operations.md#tool-selection-ladder)). **Never `Write` a flow that already has connector / connector-trigger / managed-HTTP nodes** — the rewrite clobbers their CLI-owned `bindings[]` / `inputs.detail` (invisible to `flow validate`); `Edit` in place, or re-run `node configure` as the last write. See [CAPABILITY.md — Node ownership](../CAPABILITY.md#node-ownership--who-authors-the-node).
278	
279	#### Anchoring parallel `.flow` Edits — anchor on what you Read, not on key order
280	
281	> **Do not assume a top-level key order.** The CLI does not guarantee which keys are present or in what sequence — fixtures show `runtime` before `nodes` on one flow and absent on another, and `bindings` / `variables` / `solutionId` / `projectId` / `metadata` appear in varying positions. Any anchor of the form "closing `]` + the NEXT top-level key" is coupled to that ordering and will silently break across CLI versions or between flows. **Anchor on the target array's OWN key instead — you just `Read` the file at the top of T2, so anchor to text that read actually contains.**
282	
283	Anchor each Edit using its target array's own opening key, located in the text you just Read — not adjacency to a neighbor key. The catch: `"nodes": [` and `"edges": [` are NOT unique in the file. They recur **inside inline `definitions[]`** (an HTTP v2 / agent / subprocess definition embeds its own nested `nodes`/`edges`) **and inside any `subflows.<id>` block** (each subflow holds its own `nodes`/`edges`) — so even a small flow can carry several copies. The reliable, version-independent discriminator is **indentation: the top-level array sits at 2-space indent; every nested one is deeper.** `"definitions": [` and the top-level `"layout": {` appear once each, so they need no disambiguation.
284	
285	| Edit target | Anchor on (from the text you Read) | How to insert |
286	|---|---|---|
287	| Append to `nodes[]` | The **2-space-indented** `\n  "nodes": [` (the top-level array — deeper-indented `"nodes": ["` inside definitions do not match the two-leading-space prefix) plus the `start` node's opening `{ "id": "start"`. | Insert the new node object as the first element, immediately after the `[`: `\n    { new node JSON },`. Head-insertion keeps `old_string` clear of the array's closing `]`. |
288	| Append to `edges[]` | The **2-space-indented** `\n  "edges": [`. A newly generated scaffold commonly has `\n  "edges": []`; the 2-space prefix distinguishes it from nested `edges` arrays. | When empty, replace `\n  "edges": []` with `\n  "edges": [\n    { new edge JSON }\n  ]`. When non-empty, anchor through the first edge and insert the new edge as the first element. |
289	| Append to `definitions[]` | `"definitions": [` plus the first definition's opening bytes. Top-level `definitions[]` is the only one in the file, so this is reliably unique. | Insert the new definition right after the opening `[`, as the first element. Never anchor on whatever key follows `definitions` — that key varies (`runtime`, `bindings`, `variables`, `layout`, depending on CLI version and what the flow contains). |
290	| Add an entry to `layout.nodes` | `"layout": {\n    "nodes": {\n      "start":` — `start` is the always-present trigger and the first key under `layout.nodes` in newly generated flows. The top-level `"layout": {` is the only one. | `"layout":` + `"start":` jointly disambiguate. Insert `"<newId>": { ... },\n      ` before `"start":`. CLI-owned nodes added via `node add` already have a `layout.nodes` entry — only add entries for nodes you author by hand (e.g. End). |
291	
292	**Why head-insertion.** Inserting the new element right after the array's opening `[` means the `old_string` never includes the array's closing `]` — so it cannot collide with a closing `]` from a nested object (`form.sections[].fields[]`), and it never references a sibling top-level key whose position is not guaranteed. JSON array element order is not semantically significant for `nodes` / `edges` / `definitions`, so head vs. tail insertion is equivalent; `flow format` normalizes layout regardless.
293	
294	**Disjointness rule.** Two parallel Edits MUST anchor on DIFFERENT top-level arrays — nodes-Edit on the top-level `nodes[]`, edges-Edit on the top-level `edges[]`, definitions-Edit on `definitions[]`, layout-Edit on `layout.nodes`. Because each anchors on its own array (not a shared boundary), the parallel Edits never overlap — provided each anchor is unique first (see below).
295	
296	**Pre-flight uniqueness check.** Before submitting an Edit, confirm your `old_string` appears **exactly once** in the file you Read. `"definitions": [` and the top-level `"layout": {` are reliably unique. `"nodes": [` and `"edges": [` are NOT — they recur inside inline definitions and subflows, so anchor on the **2-space-indented** occurrence and extend through the first element's opening (e.g. `"id": "start"`) until the match count is one. Never anchor on a bare bracket shape, and never assume the first textual occurrence is the top-level one.
297	
298	**Safer fallback when in doubt:** serialize the Edits across two turns. One extra turn is cheaper than a failed-Edit recovery loop (which forces a re-Read, a re-derived anchor, and a re-submit).
299	
300	**Or skip the anchoring problem:** `scripts/flow_edit.py` and `scripts/flow_compose.py` parse the file and rewrite the arrays directly, so no `old_string` has to be unique. One call per node, edge, variable, or composite rewrite — see [editing-operations-json.md](editing-operations-json.md) for the per-operation flags. `Edit` remains the right tool for a small in-place value change you want to show as a diff.
301	
302	See [shared/file-format.md — Top-level structure](../../shared/file-format.md#top-level-structure) for which top-level keys exist and the note that their order is not guaranteed.
303	
304	> **Intra-turn ordering.** If a parallel `Edit` fails with "file not read," split `Read` into its own turn (cost: +1 turn).
305	
306	### Node ownership recap
307	
308	> **Before each node, classify it as user-owned or CLI-owned (see [CAPABILITY.md — Node ownership](../CAPABILITY.md#node-ownership--who-authors-the-node)). Connector activities, connector triggers, and `core.action.http.v2` are CLI-only — use `uip maestro flow node add` + `uip maestro flow node configure`, never Edit. Hand-writing these will fail `flow validate`.**
309	
310	Edit `<ProjectName>.flow` directly in the project root. The `bindings_v2.json` file is also in the project root for resource bindings.
311	
312	> **Tool selection by ownership.** Use `Edit` for in-place changes to user-owned nodes; `Write` only when ≥70% of nodes change **and the flow has no CLI-owned nodes** (a full-file `Write` over connector / managed-HTTP nodes clobbers their `bindings[]` — see the Step 4 `Write` note above). For CLI-owned nodes (above), use `uip maestro flow node add` + `node configure` — see the relevant plugin's `impl.md` for the full configuration workflow. Inline-agent project scaffolding uses `uip agent init --inline-in-flow`, but inline-agent flow node/wiring edits are direct `.flow` JSON (the agent node itself is user-owned).
313	
314	Read [editing-operations.md](editing-operations.md) for strategy selection and per-operation recipes.
315	
316	> **Self-check before each mutation:** name the tool you're about to use. If the answer isn't `Edit`, `Write`, or `uip maestro flow ...` — STOP and ask the user (per the dropdown question rule in [SKILL.md](../../../SKILL.md)). `python`, `node`, `jq`, `sed`, `awk`, and shell heredocs are a last resort and require explicit user approval after you've surfaced the trade-offs. See [editing-operations.md — Tool Selection Ladder](editing-operations.md#tool-selection-ladder).
317	
318	For each node type, follow the relevant plugin's `impl.md` for node-specific inputs, JSON structure, and configuration. The operations guides cover the mechanics (how to add/remove/wire); the plugins cover the semantics (what inputs and model fields each node type needs).
319	
320	## Step 5 — Validate **[T3 — chain with Step 6, plus any T1 `node configure`]**
321	
322	### Canonical T3 chain — issue this as ONE `Bash` call
323	
324	```bash
325	uip maestro flow node configure "<ProjectName>.flow" "<httpNodeId>" --detail '<DETAIL_JSON>' --output json \
326	  && uip maestro flow validate "<ProjectName>.flow" --output json \
327	  && uip maestro flow format "<ProjectName>.flow" --output json
328	```
329	
330	`<DETAIL_JSON>` is node-type-specific — the schema is owned by each CLI-owned node's plugin, not duplicated here: HTTP → [http/impl.md](plugins/http/impl.md#critical-use-node-configure), connectors → [connector/impl.md](plugins/connector/impl.md), connector triggers → [connector-trigger/impl.md](plugins/connector-trigger/impl.md). Tail-append one `node configure` per CLI-owned node added in T1, using the node IDs captured from T1's chained output. Drop the entire `node configure` segment if no CLI-owned nodes exist.
331	
332	> **The plugin `impl.md` is authoritative — follow its full procedure, not just its `--detail` schema, and let it override this turn map.** A plugin may prescribe steps the three-turn collapse does not show — most importantly a **pre-`configure` live fetch** whose output you must read before you can author `--detail` (the value depends on the live response, so it cannot be guessed or copied from a doc example). When `impl.md` defines such a step, run it in its **own turn before T3** and build `--detail` from its result; do not batch it into the chain, skip it, or hand-author the payload. An empty or static base response is expected for these steps and is not a signal the step is unavailable. This is general to every CLI-owned node type — defer to the owning `impl.md` rather than assuming static config.
333	
334	Chain `python3 scripts/audit_flow.py "<ProjectName>.flow"` into the same call, before `validate` — it reports the defects `validate` does not catch (wiring, `=js:` fields, Jint constructs, resource bindings, runtime gaps) while you are still in T3.
335	
336	**On validate failure:** one `Edit` turn to fix, then re-chain `validate && format` in one Bash. Do not validate after every individual Edit during T2 — intermediate states are expected to be invalid.
337	
338	> **A passing exit code with warnings is NOT done.** `flow validate` returns 0 even when `Data.Warnings` is non-empty — read the warnings, don't just check the exit code. The connector-keyword warning (`node "…" mentions the "<connector>" connector keyword but uses the generic Managed HTTP type core.action.http.v2 with no connection binding`) means the flow took the brand-name shortcut and will run against an undefined endpoint at debug time — resolve it by switching to the connector before reporting the flow complete (see [SKILL.md rule #3](../../../SKILL.md#critical-rules-universal) and the anti-pattern list). Treat this class of warning as a build failure for your own definition of "done."
339	
340	### Common error categories
341	
342	- **Missing targetPort** — every edge needs a `targetPort` string
343	- **Missing definition** — every `type:typeVersion` in nodes needs a matching `definitions` entry
344	- **Invalid node/edge references** — `sourceNodeId`/`targetNodeId` must reference existing node `id`s
345	- **Duplicate IDs** — node and edge `id`s must be unique
346	
347	## Step 6 — Format node layout **[T3 — chained tail of Step 5]**
348	
349	This is the last segment of the [canonical T3 chain](#canonical-t3-chain--issue-this-as-one-bash-call) above. After validation passes, format must run before publishing or debugging (see "Always run `flow format` after edits" in [the Author capability index](../CAPABILITY.md)). Format:
350	
351	- Arranges nodes horizontally (left-to-right) using ELK with `nodeSpacing: 96`, anchored to the leftmost node's original position
352	- Sets each non-stickyNote node's `size` by its canvas shape so Studio Web renders it correctly: inline agents (`shape: rectangle`) → `{ "width": 288, "height": 96 }`, containers (loops/groups) → `{ "width": 560, "height": 320 }`, everything else (incl. referenced `uipath.core.agent.<guid>`) → `{ "width": 96, "height": 96 }` (skipping this leaves stale dimensions intact and produces misshapen nodes — the MST-9061 failure mode)
353	- Recurses into subflows and rewrites `subflows[<id>].layout`
354	- Backfills missing `position`/`size` entries
355	
356	Standalone (only if not chained from Step 5):
357	
358	```bash
359	uip maestro flow format <ProjectName>.flow --output json
360	```
361	
362	## Completion Output
363	
364	When you finish building the flow, report to the user:
365	
366	1. **File path** of the `.flow` file created
367	2. **What was built** — summary of nodes added, edges wired, and logic implemented
368	3. **Validation status** — whether `flow validate` passes (or remaining errors if unresolvable)
369	4. **Format status** — confirm `flow format` was run
370	5. **Mock placeholders** — list any `core.logic.mock` nodes that need to be replaced, and which skill to use
371	6. **Missing connections** — any connector nodes that need connections the user must create
372	7. **What's next** — ask the user, presenting the dropdown below (see the dropdown question rule in [SKILL.md](../../../SKILL.md))
373	
374	### What's next dropdown
375	
376	Authoring terminates here. Each option below hands off to Operate — read [operate/CAPABILITY.md](../../operate/CAPABILITY.md) for the command sequence.
377	
378	| Option | What it does |
379	| --- | --- |
380	| **Publish to Studio Web** (default) | Push the solution to Studio Web so the user can visualize, edit, and publish from the browser. |
381	| **Debug the solution** | Execute the flow end-to-end against real systems. Confirm consent first — debug has real side effects (see the consent-before-debug rule in [SKILL.md](../../../SKILL.md)). |

1	# HITL Node — Planning
2	
3	The flow needs to pause for a human to review, approve, or fill in data. Two node types serve this need — choose based on form complexity and whether an app already exists.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Which HITL Node to Use
8	
9	| Use case | Node type | Form source |
10	| --- | --- | --- |
11	| Inline form designed right now (fields + outcomes defined in the flow) | `uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form` | Schema embedded in node inputs — no app needed |
12	| Existing coded app or Action Center app | `uipath.human-in-the-loop.coded-action-app` | Deployed app from Orchestrator |
13	
14	**Prefer `uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form`** for new flows. It is an OOTB node — no registry discovery, no app publishing, no tenant dependency.
15	
16	---
17	
18	## Option 1 — `uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form` (Inline Schema — OOTB)
19	
20	Node type: `uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form`
21	Available: always — no `uip login` or registry pull required.
22	
23	### When to Select
24	
25	| Situation | Select? |
26	| --- | --- |
27	| Manager approval before processing | Yes |
28	| Human reviews extracted data before submission | Yes |
29	| Human resolves exceptions the automation cannot handle | Yes |
30	| Need a quick form with specific fields and outcomes | Yes |
31	| Existing coded/Action Center app should be used | No — use Option 2 |
32	| Fully automated processing, no human involvement | No |
33	
34	### Ports
35	
36	| Input port | Output port |
37	| --- | --- |
38	| `input` | `outcome-completed` |
39	
40	**The output port must be wired.** A node with no edge on `outcome-completed` blocks the flow indefinitely.
41	
42	### Output Variables
43	
44	- `$vars.{nodeId}.output` — object containing all output and inOut fields the human filled in
45	- `$vars.{nodeId}.output.{fieldName}` — individual field value
46	- `$vars.{nodeId}.status` — selected outcome's action value (`"Continue"` or `"End"`)
47	
48	### Schema Design
49	
50	The schema defines what the human sees and provides. Three field categories:
51	
52	| Category | Human can… | Use for |
53	| --- | --- | --- |
54	| `inputs` | Read only | Context the human needs to decide |
55	| `outputs` | Write | Data the automation needs back |
56	| `inOuts` | Read + modify | Fields the human can see and optionally correct |
57	
58	Outcomes are the action buttons (e.g., Approve/Reject). First outcome is primary.
59	
60	**In the architectural plan**, describe the schema:
61	```
62	inputs:   [invoiceId (string), amount (number)]
63	outputs:  [decision (string, required)]
64	outcomes: [Approve, Reject]
65	priority: Low
66	```
67	
68	Full JSON format and conversion examples: see [`uipath-human-in-the-loop` skill](../../../../../../uipath-human-in-the-loop/references/hitl-node-quickform.md).
69	
70	> **Note:** Skills are self-contained — cross-skill references are for documentation context only. The agent uses the `uipath-human-in-the-loop` skill to implement HITL nodes; this planning guide is for topology selection only.
71	
72	### Wiring Pattern
73	
74	```
75	[Upstream] -> [HITL] ->|outcome-completed| [Continue]
76	```
77	
78	### Common Topology Patterns
79	
80	**Approval gate:**
81	```
82	Trigger -> Fetch Data -> HITL (review) ->|outcome-completed| Decision (approved?) ->
83	  true: Script (process) -> End
84	  false: Script (log rejection) -> End
85	```
86	
87	**Exception escalation:**
88	```
89	Trigger -> Process -> Decision (confidence ok?) ->
90	  true: Continue -> End
91	  false: HITL (exception review) ->|outcome-completed| Script (retry with human input) -> End
92	```
93	
94	### Planning Annotation
95	
96	In the node table:
97	```
98	| hitlReview | Invoice Review | human-task | uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form | inputs: [invoiceId, amount] outputs: [decision] outcomes: [Approve, Reject] | output, status |
99	```
100	
101	---
102	
103	## Option 2 — `uipath.core.human-task.{key}` (App-Based)
104	
105	Node type: `uipath.core.human-task.{key}`
106	Available: tenant-specific resource — requires `uip login` + `uip maestro flow registry pull`.
107	
108	### When to Select
109	
110	Use when there is an existing coded app or Action Center app that should be the task form.
111	
112	### Ports
113	
114	| Input port | Output port |
115	| --- | --- |
116	| `input` | `output` |
117	
118	### Output Variables
119	
120	- `$vars.{nodeId}.output` — form data submitted by the user
121	- `$vars.{nodeId}.error` — error details if execution fails
122	
123	### Discovery
124	
125	**Published (tenant registry):**
126	
127	```bash
128	uip maestro flow registry pull --force
129	uip maestro flow registry search "uipath.core.human-task" --output json
130	```
131	
132	**In-solution (local, no login required):**
133	
134	```bash
135	uip maestro flow registry list --local --output json
136	uip maestro flow registry get "<node-type>" --local --output json
137	```
138	
139	Run from inside the flow project directory. Discovers sibling projects in the same `.uipx` solution.
140	
141	### Planning Annotation
142	
143	- If the app exists: note as `resource: <name> (human-task)`
144	- If it does not exist: note as `[CREATE NEW] <description>` with skill `uipath-coded-apps`, use `core.logic.mock` placeholder

1	# HITL Node — Implementation
2	
3	Two node types implement human-in-the-loop checkpoints. Choose based on whether you need an inline form or an existing deployed app.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Option 1 — `uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form` (Inline Schema — OOTB)
8	
9	This is the preferred option. No registry pull, no app publishing, no tenant dependency. Write the node directly into the `.flow` file as JSON.
10	
11	**Full implementation guide, JSON examples, and schema conversion rules:**
12	→ [`uipath-human-in-the-loop` skill — hitl-node-quickform.md](../../../../../../uipath-human-in-the-loop/references/hitl-node-quickform.md)
13	
14	> **Note:** Skills are self-contained. This cross-skill reference is for documentation context only. The agent uses the `uipath-human-in-the-loop` skill to implement HITL nodes. This implementation guide is for implementation-phase topology resolution only — not for schema design or node writing.
15	
16	### Adding / Editing
17	
18	For add, delete, and wiring procedures, see [editing-operations.md](../../editing-operations.md). **Use `Edit` / `Write` for HITL node authoring.** Do not use the dedicated HITL CLI for this non-carve-out structural edit. Wire the `outcome-completed` port after adding the node.
19	
20	### Quick Reference
21	
22	**Node JSON (minimum viable):**
23	
24	```json
25	{
26	  "id": "hitlReview1",
27	  "type": "uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form",
28	  "typeVersion": "1.0",
29	  "display": { "label": "Invoice Review" },
30	  "inputs": {
31	    "schema": {
32	      "schemaId": "<uuid>",
33	      "fields": [
34	        { "id": "invoiceid", "label": "Invoice ID", "type": "text",   "direction": "input", "binding": "vars.fetchInvoice.output.invoiceId" },
35	        { "id": "amount",    "label": "Amount",     "type": "number", "direction": "input", "binding": "vars.fetchInvoice.output.amount" },
36	        { "id": "decision",  "label": "Decision",   "type": "text",   "direction": "output", "variable": "vars.decision" }
37	      ],
38	      "outcomes": [
39	        { "id": "approve", "name": "Approve", "type": "string", "isPrimary": true,  "action": "Continue" },
40	        { "id": "reject",  "name": "Reject",  "type": "string", "isPrimary": false, "action": "End" }
41	      ]
42	    },
43	    "recipient": { "channels": ["Email", "ActionCenter"], "connections": {}, "assignee": { "type": "group" } },
44	    "priority": "Low"
45	  },
46	  "outputs": {
47	    "output": {
48	      "type": "object",
49	      "description": "Task result data",
50	      "source": "=result",
51	      "var": "output",
52	      "properties": {
53	        "decision": { "type": "string" },
54	        "Action":   { "type": "string", "enum": ["Approve", "Reject"], "default": "Approve" }
55	      }
56	    },
57	    "status": {
58	      "type": "string",
59	      "description": "Task completion status",
60	      "source": "=result.Action",
61	      "var": "status",
62	      "enum": ["Approve", "Reject"],
63	      "default": "Approve"
64	    }
65	  }
66	}
67	```
68	
69	**Field format rules:**
70	- **Input fields**: `binding: "vars.<nodeId>.output.<field>"` (raw path, no `=js:$` prefix). No `variable` property on input fields.
71	- **Output fields**: `variable: "vars.<globalName>"` (`vars.` prefix required). No `binding`.
72	- **InOut fields**: both `binding` and `variable`, same formats as above.
73	- `schemaId` (not `id`) at the schema level — generate a fresh UUID.
74	- `typeVersion` — always `"1.0"` for `uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form`. **Do not run `registry get` to derive this value; do not use `"1.1"` or any other version.** The OOTB HITL node version is stable at `1.0`.
75	- No `model` block on node instances — only the definition carries it.
76	
77	**outputs block**: only `output` (with `properties` for output/inOut fields + `Action` outcome) and `status` (with `enum`/`default` from outcomes). No per-field `custom: true` entries.
78	
79	**Ports:** `input` (target) → `outcome-completed` (source, label: Completed)
80	
81	**Output variables:**
82	- `$vars.{nodeId}.output` — object with all `output` / `inOut` field values, keyed by **field `id`**
83	- `$vars.{nodeId}.output.{fieldId}` — individual field value (e.g. `$vars.hitlReview1.output.decision`)
84	- `$vars.{nodeId}.status` — selected outcome name (e.g. `"Approve"`, `"Reject"`)
85	- `$vars.{globalId}` — workflow-global alias; `globalId` is `field.variable` with `vars.` stripped. **Do not use this in scripts — always use `$vars.{nodeId}.output.{fieldId}` instead.**
86

1	# Script Node — Implementation
2	
3	## Node Type
4	
5	`core.action.script`
6	
7	## Registry validation
8	
9	```bash
10	uip maestro flow registry get core.action.script --output json
11	```
12	
13	Confirm: input port `input`, output port `success`, required input `script` (string, non-empty). See [Action Node Structure — Registry validation](../../../../shared/action-nodes.md#registry-validation) for the shared pattern.
14	
15	## JSON structure
16	
17	Follow the [Action Node Structure — Standard JSON skeleton](../../../../shared/action-nodes.md#standard-json-skeleton). The script-specific input is a single `script` string:
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "inputs": {
22	    "script": "const items = $vars.fetchData.output.body.items;\nconst total = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.amount, 0);\nreturn { total, count: items.length };"
23	  }
24	}
25	```
26	
27	## Adding and editing
28	
29	See [Action Node Structure — Adding and editing procedures](../../../../shared/action-nodes.md#adding-and-editing-procedures). The script node uses the standard input port `input` and output port `success`; no plugin-specific wiring.
30	
31	## Script rules
32	
33	1. **Top-level body — no `function main()` wrapper.** Node runs the `script` text directly (as a function body); a wrapper is never called → `output` null. Read workflow variables via `$vars.<variableId>` and upstream node outputs via `$vars.<nodeId>.output`; end with top-level `return {…}`. Not a coded Function: no `main`, no injected args.
34	   - Correct: `const n = $vars.ixp1.output.field; return { n };`
35	   - Wrong: `function main({ ixp1 }) { … }`
36	2. **Must `return` an object** — `return { key: value }`, not a bare scalar. The return value becomes `$vars.<nodeId>.output`.
37	3. **`$vars` is a global** — use it directly: `return { upper: $vars.customerName.toUpperCase() }`
38	4. **JavaScript ES2020 (Jint engine)** — see [variables-and-expressions.md](../../../../shared/variables-and-expressions.md) for supported features and Jint constraints.
39	5. **No `console.log`** — `console` is not available. Use `return { debug: value }` to inspect values.
40	6. **No external calls** — use the HTTP node or a connector node for API calls.
41	7. **30-second timeout** — long-running computations will be killed.
42	8. **Never name a variable `aggregate`** — reserved host global. On any `Identifier 'X' has already been declared`, rename `X`.
43	
44	**Script:** `python3 scripts/lint_jint.py <ProjectName>.flow` checks rules 1, 2, 5, 6 and 8 above (plus the wider unsupported-construct list) across every script node and `=js:` expression in the file. The 30-second timeout is a runtime property and is not statically checkable.
45	
46	## Common patterns
47	
48	### Transform and return
49	
50	```javascript
51	const items = $vars.fetchData.output.body.items;
52	const filtered = items.filter(i => i.status === "active");
53	return { items: filtered, count: filtered.length };
54	```
55	
56	### Build a payload for a downstream node
57	
58	```javascript
59	return {
60	  subject: `Order ${$vars.orderId} - Confirmation`,
61	  body: `Your order of ${$vars.orderTotal} has been processed.`,
62	  recipient: $vars.customerEmail
63	};
64	```
65	
66	### Error check from upstream
67	
68	```javascript
69	const error = $vars.httpCall.error;
70	if (error) {
71	  return { hasError: true, message: error.message };
72	}
73	return { hasError: false, data: $vars.httpCall.output.body };
74	```
75	
76	### Reading a file-typed variable
77	
78	A `file` variable (bound via `uip maestro flow debug --attachment <id>=<path>`) hydrates as an **object**, not a string. Read the uploaded file's name from `.FullName`:
79	
80	```javascript
81	const doc = $vars.start.output.inputDoc; // file variable → object
82	return { fileName: doc.FullName };        // .FullName, not .name/.fileName
83	```
84	
85	Property access is **case-sensitive** — these casings resolve: `.FullName`, `.ID` (uppercase, not `.Id`), `.MimeType`, `.Metadata.size` (nested, lowercase `size`). `.name` / `.fileName` do not exist. See [variables-and-expressions.md — Runtime shape of a `file` variable](../../../../shared/variables-and-expressions.md#file-input).
86	
87	## Debug
88	
89	| Error | Cause | Fix |
90	| --- | --- | --- |
91	| Script did not return a value | Missing `return` statement | Add `return { ... }` |
92	| `output` is `null` but script has a `return` | `return` is inside an uncalled `function main(){}` wrapper | Remove wrapper; code + `return` at top level (rule 1) |
93	| Return value is not an object | Returned a scalar (`return 42`) | Wrap in object: `return { value: 42 }` |
94	| `$vars.nodeId` is undefined | Upstream node not connected or wrong ID | Check edges and node IDs |
95	| Timeout after 30s | Script too expensive | Simplify logic or split into multiple scripts |
96	| `console is not defined` | Used `console.log()` | Remove — use `return { debug: val }` instead |
97	| `fetch is not defined` | Tried to make HTTP call | Use an HTTP node or connector node instead |
98	| `[300501] Error invoking script task` with `Unexpected token` | Malformed JavaScript — `flow validate` does not parse script bodies, so syntax errors surface only at runtime. Common slip: one missing `)` in chained `(((a \|\| {}).b \|\| {}).c \|\| [])` guards | Balance parentheses; check with `node -e "new Function(<script>)"` before validate |
99	| `Identifier 'X' has already been declared` | `X` collides with a runtime-injected global (known: `aggregate`) | Rename `X` (e.g. `agg`) |
100

16	
17	### Without Output Mapping
18	
19	```json

22	  "type": "core.control.end",
23	  "typeVersion": "<DEFINITION_VERSION>",

62	| --- | --- | --- |
63	| Missing output mapping | `out` variable not mapped on this End node | Add `outputs.{varId}.source` expression for every `out` variable |
64	| Output expression unresolvable | `$vars` reference points to unreachable node | Ensure the node is upstream and connected via edges |

55	      "description": "<plugin-specific description>",

57	      "var": "output"
58	    },

1	# HITL QuickForm Node — Direct JSON Reference
2	
3	The agent writes the `uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form` node directly into the `.flow` file as JSON. **Direct JSON is the default.** A CLI opt-in is available when the user explicitly requests it, or as a fallback if direct JSON writing fails — see [CLI reference: uip maestro flow hitl add](../../uipath-maestro-flow/references/shared/cli-commands.md#uip-maestro-flow-hitl-add).
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Step 1 — Extract the Schema Through Conversation
8	
9	Before designing the schema, ask these focused questions if the business description doesn't answer them. **Ask all missing ones in a single message — never one at a time.**
10	
11	| What you need to know | Question to ask |
12	|---|---|
13	| What the reviewer sees | "What information does the reviewer need to make their decision?" |
14	| What they fill in | "Does the reviewer need to enter any data, or just click Approve/Reject?" |
15	| What actions they take | "What are the named actions — e.g. Approve/Reject, or something domain-specific like Accept/Negotiate/Decline?" |
16	
17	**Common business descriptions → schema translations:**
18	
19	| Business description | Schema shape |
20	|---|---|
21	| "Human reviews and approves/rejects an invoice" | `inputs: [invoiceId, amount]`, `outcomes: [Approve, Reject]` |
22	| "Reviewer checks agent-drafted email before sending" | `inputs: [draftEmail, recipientName]`, `inOuts: [emailBody]`, `outcomes: [Approve, Reject]` |
23	| "Escalate to human when confidence < 0.7" | `inputs: [agentReasoning, confidenceScore]`, `outputs: [action, notes]`, `outcomes: [Retry, Skip, Escalate]` |
24	| "Human fills in missing vendor data" | `inputs: [rawExtract]`, `outputs: [vendorName, costCenter]`, `outcomes: [Submit]` |
25	| "Approve before writing to ServiceNow" | `inputs: [proposedChange, targetSystem]`, `inOuts: [finalValue]`, `outcomes: [Approve, Reject]` |
26	
27	---
28	
29	## Step 1b — Discover Upstream Variables
30	
31	Before designing input field bindings, read **both** `workflow.variables.nodes` and `workflow.variables.globals` from the `.flow` file.
32	
33	### Node outputs (`variables.nodes`)
34	
35	Each entry exposes exactly what `$vars` paths are available:
36	
37	```json
38	{ "id": "fetchInvoice.output", "type": "object", "binding": { "nodeId": "fetchInvoice", "outputId": "output" } }
39	```
40	
41	The `id` field is the `$vars` path — `fetchInvoice.output` → `$vars.fetchInvoice.output`. Nested field access appends `.fieldName` (e.g., `$vars.fetchInvoice.output.invoiceId`).
42	
43	> **Binding path key = upstream script output key, not the HITL field `id`.** The HITL field `id` identifies the form field (lowercase, used for rendering). The binding path key is the property name in the upstream script's `return` statement. These are different things. If the script returns `{ supplierName: "Acme" }` and you give the HITL field `"id": "suppliername"`, the correct binding is `vars.fetchSupplier.output.supplierName` — NOT `vars.fetchSupplier.output.suppliername`. The field `id` is irrelevant to the binding path. Always look at the upstream script source to derive the key, never at the HITL field schema you are writing.
44	
45	**outputId by node type:**
46	
47	| Node type | outputId | Access pattern |
48	|---|---|---|
49	| HTTP node | `output` | `$vars.{nodeId}.output.body.{field}` |
50	| Script node | `output` | `$vars.{nodeId}.output.{field}` |
51	| Prior HITL node | `output`, `status` | `$vars.{nodeId}.output.{field}` |
52	| Agent node | `output` | `$vars.{nodeId}.output.content` |
53	| Trigger (manual) | `output` | `$vars.start.output.{field}` |
54	
55	### Flow-level globals (`variables.globals`)
56	
57	Also read `workflow.variables.globals`. Each entry has an `id` that maps directly to a `$vars` reference — no node prefix, no `.output` segment:
58	
59	```json
60	{ "id": "customerName", "direction": "in", "type": "string" }
61	```
62	
63	→ HITL binding: `"vars.customerName"` (no `=js:$` prefix — HITL binding is a raw path)
64	
65	**When to use globals instead of node outputs:** When data was declared as a flow-level input variable (e.g. the trigger passes it as a named parameter via `triggerNodeId`), it lives in `globals` with `direction: "in"`. Bind directly to `vars.<globalId>` — do not add `.output` or a node prefix.
66	
67	| Source | HITL `binding` format | Expression format (other nodes) |
68	|---|---|---|
69	| Node output | `vars.<nodeId>.output.<field>` | `=js:$vars.<nodeId>.output.<field>` |
70	| Flow global (`direction: "in"`) | `vars.<globalId>` | `=js:$vars.<globalId>` |
71	
72	> **`binding` vs `variable` prefix rule:** `binding` (input/inOut fields) uses the full path starting with `vars.` because it references an existing variable path. `variable` (output/inOut fields) uses `vars.<name>` — the `vars.` prefix is required; it declares the global variable name.
73	
74	For the full variable system, see → [How $vars paths are constructed in Flow](../../uipath-maestro-flow/references/shared/variables-and-expressions.md)
75	
76	---
77	
78	## Step 2 — Design the Schema
79	
80	The node schema uses `fields[]` entries inside `inputs.schema`. Use these conceptual roles to plan the fields before writing the node JSON:
81	
82	| Role | `direction` value | Human can… | Use for |
83	|---|---|---|---|
84	| Input field | `"input"` | Read only | Context the human needs to make a decision |
85	| Output field | `"output"` | Write | Data the automation needs back |
86	| InOut field | `"inOut"` | Read + modify | Data the human can see and optionally correct |
87	
88	**Supported field types:** `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `date`, `file`
89	
90	**Design rules:**
91	- Input fields: everything the human needs to decide — IDs, amounts, context; bind to upstream node output via `binding`
92	- Output fields: only what downstream nodes actually use; set `required: true` for mandatory outputs
93	- `outcomes`: use domain-specific names (Approve/Reject, not just Submit)
94	- Keep it focused — don't add fields the automation won't use
95	
96	**Show the designed schema to the user and confirm before writing the node.**
97	
98	---
99	
100	## Full Node JSON
101	
102	```json
103	{
104	  "id": "invoiceReview1",
105	  "type": "uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form",
106	  "typeVersion": "1.0",
107	  "display": { "label": "Invoice Review" },
108	  "inputs": {
109	    "title": "Invoice Review",
110	    "recipient": {
111	      "channels": ["Email", "ActionCenter"],
112	      "connections": {},
113	      "assignee": { "type": "group" }
114	    },
115	    "priority": "Low",
116	    "schema": {
117	      "schemaId": "a3f7c2d1-8b4e-4f9a-b2c5-6d8e1f3a7b9c",
118	      "fields": [
119	        {
120	          "id": "invoiceid",
121	          "label": "Invoice ID",
122	          "type": "string",
123	          "direction": "input",
124	          "binding": "vars.fetchInvoice.output.invoiceId"
125	        },
126	        {
127	          "id": "amount",
128	          "label": "Amount",
129	          "type": "number",
130	          "direction": "input",
131	          "binding": "vars.fetchInvoice.output.amount"
132	        },
133	        {
134	          "id": "notes",
135	          "label": "Notes",
136	          "type": "string",
137	          "direction": "output",
138	          "variable": "vars.notes",
139	          "required": false
140	        },
141	        {
142	          "id": "decision",
143	          "label": "Decision",
144	          "type": "string",
145	          "direction": "output",
146	          "variable": "vars.decision",
147	          "required": true
148	        }
149	      ],
150	      "outcomes": [
151	        { "id": "approve", "name": "Approve", "type": "string", "isPrimary": true,  "action": "Continue" },
152	        { "id": "reject",  "name": "Reject",  "type": "string", "isPrimary": false, "action": "End" }
153	      ]
154	    }
155	  },
156	  "outputs": {
157	    "output": {
158	      "type": "object",
159	      "description": "Task result data",
160	      "source": "=result",
161	      "var": "output",
162	      "properties": {
163	        "notes":    { "type": "string" },
164	        "decision": { "type": "string" },
165	        "Action":   { "type": "string", "enum": ["Approve", "Reject"], "default": "Approve" }
166	      }
167	    },
168	    "status": {
169	      "type": "string",
170	      "description": "Task completion status",
171	      "source": "=result.Action",
172	      "var": "status",
173	      "enum": ["Approve", "Reject"],
174	      "default": "Approve"
175	    }
176	  }
177	}
178	```
179	
180	**Required fields:** `id`, `type`, `typeVersion`. Position goes in the top-level `layout.nodes` object (keyed by node id), not on the node itself.
181	
182	**Node ID rule:** camelCase from the label, strip non-alphanumeric, append `1` (increment to `2`, `3`... until unique among existing node IDs). Example: `"Invoice Review"` → `invoiceReview1`.
183	
184	---
185	
186	## Definition Entry
187	
188	Every `.flow` file must have one definition entry for `uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form` in `workflow.definitions`. Add it exactly once — deduplicate by `nodeType`.
189	
190	```json

192	  "nodeType": "uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form",
193	  "version": "1.0",
194	  "category": "human-task",
195	  "description": "Fast inline approvals with inline debug",
196	  "tags": ["human-task", "hitl", "human-in-the-loop", "quick-form", "approval"],
197	  "sortOrder": 27,
198	  "display": {
199	    "label": "Quick Form",
200	    "icon": "users",
201	    "shape": "square"
202	  },
203	  "handleConfiguration": [
204	    {
205	      "position": "left",
206	      "handles": [
207	        {
208	          "id": "input",
209	          "type": "target",
210	          "handleType": "input"
211	        }
212	      ],
213	      "visible": true
214	    },
215	    {
216	      "position": "right",
217	      "handles": [
218	        { "id": "completed", "label": "Completed", "type": "source", "handleType": "output", "showButton": true, "constraints": { "forbiddenTargetCategories": ["trigger"] } }
219	      ],
220	      "visible": true
221	    }
222	  ],
223	  "model": { "type": "bpmn:UserTask", "serviceType": "Actions.HITL" },
224	  "inputDefaults": {
225	    "schema": {
226	      "fields": [],
227	      "outcomes": [{ "id": "submit", "name": "Submit", "type": "string", "isPrimary": true, "action": "Continue" }]
228	    },
229	    "recipient": {

243

245	
246	Wire the `completed` output handle to the downstream node. Edge ID format: `{sourceNodeId}-{sourcePort}-{targetNodeId}-{targetPort}` (append `-2`, `-3` on collision).

255	
256	## `variables.nodes` — Regenerate After Every Node Add/Remove
257	
258	The HITL node exposes two outputs (`output`, `status`). After adding it, **completely replace** `workflow.variables.nodes` by iterating all nodes and collecting their outputs:
259	
260	```json
261	"variables": {
262	  "nodes": [
263	    {
264	      "id": "invoiceReview1.output",
265	      "type": "object",
266	      "description": "Task result data",
267	      "binding": { "nodeId": "invoiceReview1", "outputId": "output" }
268	    },
269	    {
270	      "id": "invoiceReview1.status",
271	      "type": "string",
272	      "description": "Task completion status",
273	      "binding": { "nodeId": "invoiceReview1", "outputId": "status" }
274	    }
275	  ]
276	}

279	Include entries for **all** nodes in the flow, not just the HITL node. Replace the entire array — do not append. 281	> **Scripts must always use `$vars.<nodeId>.output.<fieldId>`.** The `field.variable` property declares a name for the global alias — do NOT use that name directly in scripts. `$vars.decision` (global alias) and `$vars.<nodeId>.output.decision` (field ID access) are different paths and only the field ID path is reliable in script nodes. 283	---
284	
285	## Canonical Field Shape (reference)
286	
287	This is the exact JSON a correctly authored QuickForm `fields[]` entry looks like for each direction. Use this as ground truth when writing or reviewing HITL nodes.
288	
289	```json
290	{
291	  "fields": [
292	    {
293	      "id": "invoiceid",
294	      "type": "number",
295	      "label": "Invoice ID",
296	      "direction": "input",
297	      "binding": "vars.fetchInvoice1.output.invoiceId"
298	    },
299	    {
300	      "id": "vendorname",
301	      "type": "string",
302	      "label": "Vendor Name",
303	      "direction": "input",
304	      "binding": "vars.fetchInvoice1.output.vendorName"
305	    },
306	    {
307	      "id": "approveddate",
308	      "type": "date",
309	      "label": "Approved Date",
310	      "direction": "output",
311	      "variable": "vars.approvedDate"
312	    },
313	    {
314	      "id": "approved",
315	      "type": "boolean",
316	      "label": "Approved",
317	      "direction": "output",
318	      "variable": "vars.approved"
319	    }
320	  ],
321	  "outcomes": [
322	    {
323	      "id": "submit",
324	      "name": "Submit",
325	      "type": "string",
326	      "action": "Continue",
327	      "isPrimary": true
328	    }
329	  ]
330	}
331	```
332	
333	**Key rules this sample encodes:**
334	- `type`: always a JS/JSON type — `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `date`, or `file`. Never `"text"`.
335	- `variable`: always `"vars.<name>"` — the `vars.` prefix is required.
336	- `binding`: input/inOut fields only; raw path (`vars.<nodeId>.output.<field>`), no `=js:$` prefix.
337	- Output/inOut fields have `variable`; input fields do not.
338	
339	---
340	
341	## Schema Conversion — Examples
342	
343	The agent translates the user's business description into the `fields[]` and `outcomes[]` arrays. No CLI needed — apply these rules directly.
344	
345	### Rules
346	
347	| What | Rule |
348	|---|---|
349	| field `id` | lowercase label, spaces→`-`, strip non-alphanumeric. `"Invoice ID"` → `"invoiceid"`, `"Due Date"` → `"due-date"` |
350	| `direction` | `inputs[]` items → `"input"`, `outputs[]` → `"output"`, `inOuts[]` → `"inOut"` |
351	| field `type` | Use the JS/JSON type: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `date`, or `file` |
352	| `binding` | **Input / inOut fields only.** Format: `"vars.<nodeId>.output.<field>"` for node outputs; `"vars.<globalId>"` for flow globals. **No `=js:$` prefix** — HITL binding is a raw path, not an expression. |

1	# HITL Business Pattern Recognition Guide
2	
3	Use this guide to decide whether a business process needs a Human-in-the-Loop node, and where to place it — even when the user has not explicitly asked for one.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## When to Recommend HITL
8	
9	Look for these signals in the business description or process context:
10	
11	### Approval gate
12	The automation produces something that requires sign-off before it can proceed.
13	
14	| Signal phrases | Examples |
15	|---|---|
16	| "approve", "sign off", "authorize", "get approval" | Invoice approval, PO sign-off, budget authorization |
17	| "four-eyes check", "dual control", "maker-checker" | Financial transactions, compliance workflows |
18	| "review before posting", "validate before sending" | CRM updates, email campaigns, database writes |
19	
20	**Insertion point:** After the automation generates the artifact to review, before it takes the action requiring approval.
21	
22	---
23	
24	### Exception escalation
25	The automation hits a case it cannot resolve autonomously and needs a human decision.
26	
27	| Signal phrases | Examples |
28	|---|---|
29	| "if uncertain / low confidence, escalate" | AI agent confidence threshold |
30	| "edge case", "anomaly", "exception handling" | Fraud alerts, out-of-policy transactions |
31	| "escalate to manager / supervisor" | Customer service workflows |
32	
33	**Insertion point:** Inside a conditional branch where the automation detects it cannot proceed alone.
34	
35	---
36	
37	### Data enrichment
38	The automation extracted or generated data that is incomplete — a human must fill in the gaps.
39	
40	| Signal phrases | Examples |
41	|---|---|
42	| "fill in missing fields", "enrich", "complete the record" | Partially extracted invoice data |
43	| "human validates / corrects" | OCR output verification |
44	| "needs human input before continuing" | Missing vendor code, unknown cost center |
45	
46	**Insertion point:** After extraction/generation, before the downstream step that requires complete data.
47	
48	---
49	
50	### Compliance and audit checkpoint
51	A regulation or internal policy requires documented human sign-off.
52	
53	| Signal phrases | Examples |
54	|---|---|
55	| "compliance", "audit trail", "regulatory sign-off" | SOX controls, GDPR consent flows |
56	| "must be reviewed by", "requires attestation" | Legal review gates, privacy impact assessments |
57	
58	**Insertion point:** At the mandated checkpoint defined by the regulation or policy.
59	
60	---
61	
62	### Write-back validation
63	An agent or automation is about to write to an external system — a human must confirm the proposed change.
64	
65	| Signal phrases | Examples |
66	|---|---|
67	| "before writing to", "before posting to", "agent writes to ServiceNow / SAP / CRM" | Any write to a system of record |
68	| "human confirms before agent acts" | Autonomous agent guard rails |
69	
70	**Insertion point:** Immediately before the write/post action.
71	
72	---
73	
74	### Agentic output review
75	An AI agent produced a document, draft, classification, or recommendation — a human must verify it before the result is used or published.
76	
77	| Signal phrases | Examples |
78	|---|---|
79	| "review AI-generated content", "human verifies before sending" | Agent-drafted emails, RCA reports, meeting summaries |
80	| "check before publishing", "validate AI output" | AI-written case notes, support ticket responses |
81	| "human in the loop for AI decisions" | Any LLM output going to a system of record or customer |
82	
83	**Insertion point:** After the agent node, before the downstream action that consumes the output.
84	
85	---
86	
87	### IT / change management approval
88	A change request or access request needs human authorization before the automation executes it.
89	
90	| Signal phrases | Examples |
91	|---|---|
92	| "CAB approval", "change request", "change window" | IT change management (ServiceNow, Jira Service Management) |
93	| "access request", "provision access", "grant permission" | Identity and access management workflows |
94	| "runbook approval", "deployment sign-off" | DevOps release gates |
95	
96	**Insertion point:** After the automation prepares the change record, before it applies the change.
97	
98	---
99	
100	### HR and offer / contract workflows
101	A document or decision with legal or HR significance must be reviewed before it is sent to a third party.
102	
103	| Signal phrases | Examples |
104	|---|---|
105	| "offer letter", "employment contract", "onboarding approval" | HR hiring workflows |
106	| "termination review", "performance decision" | HR case management |
107	| "contract terms", "counter-sign", "legal review gate" | Procurement, vendor onboarding |
108	
109	**Insertion point:** After document generation, before the document is dispatched.
110	
111	---
112	
113	### Customer communication approval
114	An automation is about to send a message on behalf of a person or brand — a human must review tone, accuracy, or content before it goes out.
115	
116	| Signal phrases | Examples |
117	|---|---|
118	| "approve before sending", "review draft email", "check before posting" | Customer support responses, marketing emails |
119	| "agent-written reply", "draft response" | Helpdesk, CRM follow-ups |
120	
121	**Insertion point:** After the draft is generated, before the send/post action.
122	
123	---
124	
125	### Financial transaction approval
126	A monetary action above a threshold or of a certain type requires human sign-off.
127	
128	| Signal phrases | Examples |
129	|---|---|
130	| "above threshold", "over limit", "exceeds budget" | PO approval, expense reimbursement over limit |
131	| "wire transfer", "payment release", "credit note" | AP/AR workflows |
132	| "price override", "discount approval" | Sales quote approval |
133	
134	**Insertion point:** After the automation determines the transaction details, before it submits the payment or posts the entry.
135	
136	---
137	
138	## When NOT to Recommend HITL
139	
140	- The process description is fully automated with no decision point (e.g. "process all invoices automatically")
141	- The human interaction is asynchronous notification only (use email/Slack activity instead)
142	- The user explicitly says no human review is needed
143	- The decision can be made by a rule or AI model with sufficient confidence
144	- The user is asking about **runtime task management** — reassigning, monitoring, cancelling, or checking the status of existing Action Center tasks. These are operational questions answered by `uip tasks` commands or the Orchestrator UI, not by adding a HITL node. A question like "how do I reassign a task sitting for 3 days?" is task administration, not automation authoring — do not recommend adding a HITL checkpoint in response.
145	
146	---
147	
148	## Proactive HITL Recommendation
149	
150	If a business description contains any of the above signals but the user has not asked for a HITL, flag it:
151	
152	> "This process includes [signal]. Before the automation [action], a human should review [data]. I recommend inserting a HITL node here — want me to add it?"
153	
154	Then proceed to Step 3 (schema design) only after the user confirms.

509	- **Flow inputs**: Add entries to `variables.nodes[]` whose `binding.nodeId` is the start node and whose `binding.outputId` names each input value — the start node "outputs" input values to downstream nodes
